claims.text: Controlled carbon doping will improve the glass-forming ability of phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys.
Controlled carbon doping will improve the thermal stability of the amorphous state in phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys.
Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 is an example of the proposed phosphorus-containing alloy baseline.
The undoped phosphorus-containing baseline can be amorphized by rapid quenching.
The undoped phosphorus-containing baseline has moderate thermal stability.
A low, controlled concentration of carbon should be introduced during alloy synthesis.
Rapid cooling by melt spinning or an equivalent method promotes amorphization in the proposed alloy.
The carbon effect should be observable at cooling rates that already yield an amorphous undoped baseline.
Carbon atoms modify the local bonding environment in the phosphorus-containing alloy.
Carbon forms additional directional, likely covalent, bonds in the alloy.
The carbon-induced bonding changes interfere with crystalline nucleation and stabilize short-range amorphous networks.
Carbon doping increases local bonding heterogeneity.
Increased bonding heterogeneity and configurational entropy disrupt long-range periodic ordering by interfering with nucleation and crystal growth.
Carbon-doped samples will have a higher crystallization-onset temperature or a lower crystallization rate than identically processed undoped samples.
Excessive carbon incorporation may produce secondary phases or carbon-rich precipitates.
The benefits to glass formation and thermal stability will occur only in a low-carbon doping regime.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant increase in amorphous fraction or crystallization-onset temperature relative to the undoped control would falsify the hypothesis.
